clue.text: Unenthusiastic lad receives a letter from abroad

indicators.note: the lad takes in, or receives, the foreign letter, so it goes inside his name

parts.note: Ted is a common short name for a boy or lad
pi is a Greek letter, so a letter from abroad

explanation.surface: A half-hearted boy gets post from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'letter' is not post but a character of a foreign alphabet, and 'receives' is the containment signal: the lad holds it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lukewarm water is tepid, and figuratively a lukewarm, half-hearted response is unenthusiastic.

clue.text: Land in border county

parts.note: in rugby and football touch is the area beyond the side boundary, the border of the pitch
Down is a county of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Property situated on the edge of a county.
explanation.walkthrough: DOWN is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland. 'In' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft's touchdown is the moment it lands on the runway.

clue.text: Works in the garden

explanation.surface: Someone is busy gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's verb 'works' is the noun meaning a factory; the second sense is the verb of setting seeds in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant is an industrial factory or works; to plant is to set something growing in the soil of a garden.

clue.text: Citadel ruined, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: a ruined fortress has fallen apart, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fortress lies wrecked, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' reads as a phrase meaning 'so to speak', but 'a manner of speaking' is the definition; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is a regional or social variety of a language, a particular way of speaking.

clue.text: Drama featuring equally a poet and an artist

parts.note: 'so' can mean equally or likewise, as in 'and so am I'
Alexander Pope was an English poet
RA stands for Royal Academician, a crossword stock artist

explanation.surface: A play in which a poet and a painter share the billing equally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Featuring' is only a link here. A soap opera is a long-running serial drama on radio or television.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera is a serialised domestic television or radio drama, originally sponsored by soap makers.

clue.text: Train a group of porpoises

explanation.surface: Teaching a pod of sea mammals.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or drill them; a school is also the collective noun for porpoises, whales or fish.

clue.text: Sum is complicated — and I do it!

indicators.note: when the phrase is complicated it is muddled, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that they can do even a tricky arithmetic problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is complicated' looks like a comment on the sum, but signals the anagram of AND I DO IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding numbers together gives a total, and an addition is such a sum.

clue.text: Cow in half-open cupboard

indicators.note: half means only the first two of the four letters of open are kept

parts.note: a press is a large cupboard for linen or clothes

explanation.surface: A farm animal stands in a cupboard left ajar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' is a verb, to intimidate. A press, in older and Irish use, is a cupboard; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow people is to subdue and intimidate them, and to oppress them is to keep them down by harsh treatment.

clue.text: "Clear out of class" I interjected

indicators.note: to interject is to throw in between, so the word for I goes between the other two parts

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of, as in ex-directory
a rate is a grade or class, as in first-rate
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone recalls interrupting to say a pupil must be allowed to leave the lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase looks like a remark made aloud, but 'Clear' is the definition, and 'interjected' tells you the number for 'I' is thrown in between the other parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate is to free someone from blame, to clear their name.

clue.text: Should we hear anything?

indicators.note: we hear tells you the word is said aloud, and a word sounding like it is entered

parts.note: ought means should, as in 'you ought to go'

explanation.surface: A question whether there is any news.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two words are pronounced alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Aught is an archaic word for anything at all, as in 'for aught I know'.

clue.text: Shameless girl gets hit

parts.note: Una is a girl's name
bashed means struck or hit hard

explanation.surface: A brazen young woman ends up being struck.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shameless is not embarrassed or abashed by anything, the plain meaning of the word.

clue.text: In second half of game, receiver finally achieves a point

indicators.note: the receiver's last letter goes in the half-game named before it
only the latter half of the game's name is kept, the first half dropped

parts.note: ping-pong is another name for table tennis

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word receiver

explanation.surface: Late in a table tennis match, the receiver at last wins a point.
explanation.walkthrough: The game is PING-PONG, whose second half PONG takes in R, the last letter of 'receiver'. 'Achieves a' is link material.
explanation.definitionFit: A prong is one of the pointed tines of a fork, so a sharp point.

clue.text: Belittle Beth, who is in trouble — it's not fair

indicators.note: words in trouble are in a mess, so their letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone protests that running down Beth, who is going through a bad time, is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' looks like Beth's plight, but it signals the anagram of BELITTLE BETH WHO; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In boxing a low punch breaks the rules, so the idiom describes any unfair or unsporting attack.

clue.text: It's strange — not even one Tory lost heart

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd
the Roman numeral I is one

indicators.note: the middle letters of the word are taken away, as a heart is the centre

parts.note: Tory is the everyday name for a British Conservative

explanation.surface: A remark that it is odd that an unusual Conservative politician became discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost heart' suggests despair but removes OR, the centre of TORY, leaving TY. The definition is a whole phrase: a thing that is strange.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddity is a peculiar thing or person, something out of the ordinary.

clue.text: For instance, the accent I had upset a reviewer

indicators.note: upset, in a down clue, turns the short form upside down so it reads upwards

parts.note: I had is shortened to I'd
a critic writes reviews

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that a critic was put out by their accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, flagged by 'For instance': an accent is one kind of the mark defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Marks added to letters to show pronunciation, like the acute or grave accent, are diacritical signs.

clue.text: Girl and boy finally meet in stable

parts.note: Con is a short form of the girl's name Constance
Stan is a boy's name

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of the word meet

explanation.surface: A romance where a girl and boy at last get together in a stable.
explanation.walkthrough: The stable seems to be a place with horses, but it is the definition, an adjective; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something constant does not change or waver, just as something stable is steady and unshifting.

clue.text: Having no sense let assets deteriorate

indicators.note: things that deteriorate go to pieces, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone senseless allows their holdings to decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having no sense' first suggests foolishness, but here the sense is taste, as in food with no flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is insipid has no flavour, lacking the sense of taste it should stimulate.

clue.text: Royalty included in the papers

indicators.note: the abbreviation is put in the word for the papers

parts.note: the press means the newspapers collectively
inc. is the abbreviation of included or inclusive

explanation.surface: Coverage of the royal family features in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Included' looks like the containment signal, but gives its abbreviation INC; 'in' is what puts it inside PRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A king's daughter belongs to the royal family, so she is one of the royalty.

clue.text: Rescue craft in drama round a 'small island

indicators.note: the drama goes round, or encloses, the single letter that follows

parts.note: Noh is classical Japanese drama
Sark is a small Channel Island

explanation.surface: A lifeboat features in a play set around a tiny island.
explanation.walkthrough: Noh is the stylised masked drama of Japan; SARK lies near Guernsey in the Channel Islands. 'In' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the Ark saved Noah's family and the animals from the Flood, a vessel of rescue.

clue.text: Unfamiliar way over the mountains

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits over, or above, the second

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a range is a line of mountains

explanation.surface: A new route across the mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: Something strange is new or unknown to you, unfamiliar.

clue.text: Several people who collect pearls

explanation.surface: Some people go pearl hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: As an old adjective divers means sundry or several; as a noun it names those who swim underwater, as pearl gatherers do.

clue.text: Taken in custody, put up in a hotel

indicators.note: the reversed word for custody sits in the word for a hotel

parts.note: an inn is a small hotel

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the word reads upwards, from the bottom

parts.note: a ward is a person in custody, or a cell for one

explanation.surface: A suspect is arrested and lodged at a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' suggests lodging a guest, but it is the upward reversal in this down clue, making DRAW; the second 'in' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Breath drawn in is breath taken in, the plain sense of the participle.

clue.text: For a break, knock about a country

indicators.note: the word for knock goes about, or around, the single letter

parts.note: to hit is to knock or strike
US is the United States, a country

explanation.surface: A traveller takes a holiday, roaming round a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock about' looks like a phrase for wandering idly, but 'knock' is HIT and 'about' puts it round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiatus is a pause or gap in continuity, an interruption in proceedings.

clue.text: He singed a beard and badly scarred fair skin

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man burnt off some whiskers and in doing so left pale skin marked.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1587 the Elizabethan seaman raided Cadiz, boasting he had singed the King of Spain's beard. 'Badly' signals the anagram of SCARRED FAIR SKIN; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cadiz raid of 1587, wrecking the Spanish fleet, is famously called singeing the King of Spain's beard.

clue.text: "Well, hello there, soldier!"

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring or well
hi is a greeting, hello there

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting to a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: A spahi was a cavalryman in the Ottoman army, later in the French army in North Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Spahis were Turkish and later Algerian cavalry troops, so the word names a soldier.

clue.text: A girl gone wrong

parts.note: a miss is a young girl

explanation.surface: A young woman has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something amiss is faulty or not as it should be, out of order.

clue.text: Affect part of London

explanation.surface: A district of the capital has an effect.
explanation.walkthrough: ACTON is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: To act upon something is to influence or affect it; Acton is also a west London district.

clue.text: Extension of play — actor to give out backing

parts.note: an extra is a minor film actor in a crowd scene

indicators.note: backing means the word for giving out is read from the end towards the start

parts.note: to emit is to give out light or sound

explanation.surface: A performer's lines in a stage play run long, while he gives out support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' sounds like support from a performer, but it is the reversal signal, giving TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, extra time is the period added to a drawn match, extending the play.

clue.text: 5's crumpled

explanation.walkthrough: 5 refers to the answer of 5 down, ADDITION, so '5's' means additions. The second sense splits the answer into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Additions are rises or increases; read as two words, something with folds in it is crumpled.

clue.text: Peers — one's missing when sitting is resumed

indicators.note: missing means these letters are taken out of what is left
resumed is read as taken back, so the word for sitting runs backwards

parts.note: a sitting of parliament or a court is a session
one is I, so one's gives I plus S

explanation.surface: Lords note that one member is absent when the House sits again.
explanation.walkthrough: Peers looks like members of the House of Lords but is a verb. 'Resumed' turns SESSION into NOISSES, and 'missing' takes out I and S to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who noses around pokes about and looks searchingly, as one who peers does.
